Mount Tai is difficult to place within a bag; this refers to the contemplation of the five unobstructed dharma-realms (*pañca-avyāghāta-dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*). This is precisely the contemplation of the universal dharma-realm (*samasta-dharmadhātu*) which serves as the basis for the four dharma-realms; it means constantly contemplating and visualizing all phenomena, both defiled and pure.
The entire body is entirely the mind of the unobstructed dharma-realm;
this contemplating wisdom is also conceived as being entirely the mind of the dharma-realm.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"To know that all phenomena are the very nature of one's own mind is to accomplish the body of wisdom, which is not realized through another."
Furthermore, Qingliang says:
"If one knows that all objects touched are mind, only then will one realize the nature of the mind.
Now, within this unobstructed dharma-realm,"
The three worlds and the four dharma-realms, comprising all phenomena—both defiled and pure—are inherently complete within it;
not a single phenomenon exists outside this dharma-realm.
Yet, this dharma-realm is entirely both this and that, with no mutual obstruction between them.
Thus one knows that every faculty and every object is entirely the unobstructed Dharma-realm.
If, within the four modes of deportment, one constantly contemplates that every faculty and every object is the infinitely layered and inexhaustible Dharma-realm.
This is the practice of the realm of the Universal Eye; this contemplation is the root of all gateways to the contemplations of samādhi.
If one constantly practices them, all the gateways to the contemplations of samādhi mentioned above will naturally manifest before one.
Whether one prefers to practice all [the methods] together or practices one or two, either way is acceptable according to one's inclination;
provided one cultivates and refines them with single-minded diligence,
if success is not achieved in one lifetime, it will certainly be perfected within three.
Furthermore, the practitioner must give rise to mental visualization;
when this visualization is attained such that it constantly manifests before them without concealment,
only then is it the true practice of the Huayan Perfect Teaching.
In the "Ten Mysterious Gates of Unobstructed Interpenetration" by the Master Qingliang, there are many instances of six phrases;
the first five phrases concern the cultivation of mental conceptions.
When it is refined until it manifests before one, one no longer thinks of further refining it;
yet, though one does not think of refining it, it constantly manifests without concealment—
only then is the sixth stage of practice accomplished.
The *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā* states:
"Contemplate it deeply and subtly so that it manifests before you, appearing with perfect clarity as the sphere of practice. Master Guishan’s commentary explains:
One contemplates until it manifests as true understanding.
Once it has manifested, one no longer contemplates;
yet, although there is no further contemplation, it remains constantly manifest and never hidden.
This is indeed the practice of true cultivation. Furthermore, Master Seung Sahn said:
"First, one must give rise to a thought so that it manifests before one;
only then should one employ the emptiness of *prajñā* to purify and eliminate it."
Thus, one immediately accomplishes inconceivable great function and enters the fruit of Buddhahood instantaneously.
If one does not give rise to the thought [of observing] but instead observes erroneously, this is a misunderstanding of the meaning of Prajñā.
Even if one were to enter emptiness in such a manner, one would still lose the path of the Perfect and Sudden.
For a practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong),
when the refinement of their cultivation reaches the point where words vanish and thoughts cease in a sudden flash of realization,
only then is it truly authentic practice— clear and distinct.
If one attains such a state,
one will constantly perceive inconceivable realms within the four modes of deportment.
May those who cultivate the Path apply their minds to this.
It is fundamentally thus, yet one fails to see it because of ignorance.
Furthermore, for those who practice the cultivation of the mind,
there may arise various types of dreams, whether virtuous or non-virtuous.
One may encounter various demonic obstacles;
various favorable or adverse conditions may manifest;
or various sounds, good or evil, may be heard.
Or various types of insects and ants may crawl over one's body;
or the body and mind may become unsettled, leading to excessive thinking and brooding;
or when entering into contemplation, various kinds of signs may appear.
One must contemplate that all things which do not correspond with the original contemplation are entirely unreal,
like dreams or illusions; or else,
one should contemplate them as being entirely one's own true mind.
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:
"One should maintain the mindfulness that all is but mind;
then objective realms will cease, and one will ultimately not be afflicted by them."
The above concludes the essential points of the Exoteric Teachings.
Second, regarding the essential points of the Esoteric Teachings,
these refer to the *Commentary on the Spiritual Transformations* (*Shenbian shuchao*).
The *Mandara-sho-shō* all judge the teachings of the dhāraṇīs to be the Esoteric Perfect [Teaching].
In the preceding Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) of the Exoteric Vehicle,
one must first awaken to the Dharma-realm of Vairocana,
and subsequently, based on that awakening, cultivate until the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra is perfected.
One attains liberation from birth and death and realizes the fruit of Buddhahood, the ten bodies of unimpeded mastery.
It is like a sick person who obtains an excellent medicinal prescription;
they must personally know the proportions of the ingredients and the methods for steaming and roasting them.
Only by compounding and wearing it can one eliminate illness and attain physical peace.
Now, as for this secret and perfect divine mantra,
all sentient beings as well as Bodhisattvas on the causal stages—
Even if one does not understand [the meaning] but merely upholds and recites it,
one will then possess the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices within the Vairocana Dharma-realm;
naturally, one shall transcend birth and death and achieve the fruit of Buddhahood as the ten bodies of unimpeded mastery.
It is like a sick person who obtains a well-compounded, wondrous medicine;
although they do not know the proportions or the rules for its compounding,
by merely taking it, their illness is naturally eliminated and their body becomes at ease.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The secret mantras and esoteric teachings of all Buddhas are understood only by Buddhas communicating with one another;
they cannot be fully penetrated by other sages."
Merely reciting and upholding it can extinguish great transgressions and enable one to swiftly ascend to the rank of a sage.
It is further said that this divine mantra is the secret seal (*guhyamudrā*) of all Buddhas;
transmitted from Buddha to Buddha, it is not to be understood by others.
The *Xian-shou Banruo Shu* states:
"Mantras are the secret dharma of all Buddhas;
they are not to be understood by those at the stage of a cause."
One should simply recite and uphold them; there is no need for forced exegesis.
Furthermore, Master Huiyuan’s *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Mantras are not necessarily exclusively the language of India."
The translators did not understand it, and therefore they did not translate it.
Furthermore, the *Tianzhu Zhiguan* states:
"Only the supreme sages are able to manifest both the exoteric and esoteric teachings."
Ordinary people are only able to propagate and manifest the Exoteric Teachings;
they cannot propagate and manifest the Esoteric Teachings.
Since antiquity, all masters have expounded upon dhāraṇīs.
The noble ones at the stage of cause cannot comprehend it;
they merely believe and uphold it to extinguish hindrances and accomplish virtues. Question: Why are the secret mantras of the Buddhas not accessible to others' understanding?

The answer states: "It is said that when the perfect understanding (*yuanjie*) and the partial understanding (*pianjie*) give rise to the incantation, the incantation loses its efficacy. Therefore, it does not apply to other interpretations;
the esoteric meaning lies herein, which one should reflect upon."
Therefore, the *Fahua chao* states:
"Because the secret dharma of all Buddhas does not manifest its meaning, it is called 'secret words' (*guhyamantra*). The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Dhāraṇī is like a wondrous medicine and also like the nectar of heaven."
It can cure the diseases of manifold delusions; those who take it will always enjoy peace and happiness.
Furthermore, in the *Naya-samgraha-sūtra*, the Tathāgata taught that there are five treasuries (*piṭaka*).
First is the Sūtra-piṭaka, which is like cow's milk.
The second, the Vinaya Piṭaka, is like curd;
the third, the Śāstra Piṭaka, is like fresh butter;
and the fourth, the Prajñā Piṭaka, is like clarified butter.
The five dharanī-piṭakas are like the finest cream (sarpis-manda);
the flavor of the finest cream is the foremost among milk, curd, and other such products.

This *dhāraṇī* for curing all diseases and bringing peace and happiness to the body and mind of all sentient beings, which was widely used in the Western Heavens (India) for healing with clarified butter (*sarpis*),
is the foremost among the sūtras, vinayas, and other scriptures.
It is capable of eliminating all transgressions and causing all sentient beings to be liberated from birth and death,
swiftly realizing the blissful Dharma-body of Nirvana.
The *Pīṭaka-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Principles) states:
The power of the nature-virtues is great and the efficacy of the secret mantras is strong;
thus, even if one's understanding and practice are inferior, liberation is swift.
A question is asked: "What about the Great Master Xianshou and others?"
While it was previously judged that only the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) and all other teachings are not,
we now judge that this dhāraṇī is likewise of the Perfect Teaching.
Would this not contradict the teachings of Xianshou and others?
It should rather state that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) has two aspects:
first, the manifest perfect, and second, the esoteric perfect.
Worthy One, based solely on the teachings of the Exoteric Vehicle,
you correctly judge the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to be of the Perfect [Teaching].
Now, regarding the *Commentary on the Divine Transformations*, the *Sub-commentary*, and the *Commentary on the Maṇḍala*:
By analogy with the Manifest [Teaching], which is judged to be Perfect, this Esoteric Teaching is likewise of the Perfect School.
Since the Manifest and Esoteric are distinct,
there is no contradiction among the various masters.
The esoteric, perfect cultivation and refinement is also divided into two parts:
first, the ritual procedures for recitation;
second, the modes of practice for attaining realization.
Furthermore, regarding the ritual procedures for initial recitation:
this refers to the practitioner of the mantra who wishes to perform the recitation according to the dharma every day.
When reciting,
one must first assume the Vajra posture, pressing the right foot upon the left thigh;
alternatively, one may sit in a relaxed posture, forming the Great Samaya Mudrā with both hands palms upturned and fully extended.
Place the right hand upon the left hand with the two thumbs touching at their nail tips,
and rest them below the navel center.
This mudrā can extinguish all forms of madness, deluded thoughts, and defiled contemplations; only when body and mind are clarified and stabilized does one enter the samādhi of the pure dharma-realm.
This means visualizing upon the crown of one's head the Sanskrit syllable *HŪṂ*.
This syllable is pervaded by radiance,
like a bright pearl or the full moon.
Having visualized this syllable:
Furthermore, with the left hand, form the Vajra-fist mudrā by pressing the thumb against the first joint at the base of the ring finger;
the remaining four fingers encircle the thumb to form a fist.
This mudrā can eliminate internal and external obstructions and defilements,
and accomplish all meritorious virtues. With the right hand holding a rosary,
one should recite the mantra of the Pure Dharma Realm twenty-one times.
The mantra is: Oṃ raṃ.

Alternatively, it is also permissible to hold only the syllable *raṃ*, which is also known as the syllable *raṃ*. [Oṃ] (Sanskrit script) [Raṃ] (Sanskrit script). This is the *oṃ* of the pure dharma-realm; the syllable *raṃ*.
Whether one contemplates or recites it,
it can cause the three karmas to become entirely pure,
and all sinful obstructions will be completely eliminated.
Furthermore, it can accomplish all supreme matters;
wherever one dwells, that place becomes entirely pure.
Even if one's clothing is impure, it becomes a pure garment.
If one has not bathed, one should bathe.
If one uses water for purification, it is not called true purification.
If one uses the syllable *raṃ* from the mind of this dharmadhātu to purify oneself, that is true purification.
This is precisely what is called ultimate purity.
Just as a single grain of an elixir of immortality can transform iron into gold,
a single syllable of the mantra transforms defilement into purity.
The verse says: "The syllable *ra* is brilliant white, adorned with a *bindu*.
In the Sanskrit script, placing a *bindu* above the syllable *ra* forms the syllable *ṝ*."
Like that bright jewel in a topknot placed upon the crown of the head,
the mantra is identical to the Dharma-realm.
Immeasurable multitudes of sins are eliminated.
In all places that are defiled by contact, one should apply this gateway of syllables.
If external conditions are not fulfilled—such as lacking water for bathing or being short of fresh, clean clothing—[one should still proceed].
Simply use this syllable *ṢRAṂ* to purify it.
If external conditions are complete,
first rinse with water and don a new, clean garment.
Furthermore, purify it with this syllable *raṃ*.
Thus, both the interior and exterior become completely pure.
The details are as explained in the various mantra ritual manuals (*vidhi-sūtra*).
Next, recite the mantra for protecting the body twenty-one times. The mantra is:
OṂ JHAḤ. Pronounce the syllable *JHA* with a retroflex sound and in the departing tone; it extinguishes the five heinous crimes, the ten evil deeds, and all karmic obstructions.
It can eliminate all manner of suffering from illness, calamities, obstacles, and evil dreams;
it can dispel the influence of malevolent spirits, ghosts, and deities,
as well as all inauspicious occurrences, and is able to accomplish every supreme undertaking.
It causes all aspirations to be fully realized.
This mantra is the heart-essence of all Buddhas;
if a person recites it with single-minded devotion even once, they will be able to protect themselves.
All ghosts, spirits, and celestial Māras will not dare to approach or invade.
Reciting it twice can protect one's companions;
reciting it three times can protect all those within a single household.
Reciting it four times can protect the people within a single city;
reciting it up to seven times can protect the people of the four continents, as explained in detail in the *Mañjuśrī-mūla-ekākṣara-mantra-sūtra*.
It is also permissible to recite each of the two preceding mantras one hundred and eight times.
Next, recite the Six-Syllable Great Illumination Mantra one hundred and eight times.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ maṇipadme hūṃ. If one recites this mantra, wherever one dwells, there will be an assembly of immeasurable Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.
Furthermore, it possesses immeasurable dharma-gates of samādhi.
Those who recite and uphold it shall attain liberation for seven generations of their lineage;
even the various worms within their bellies shall attain the rank of a bodhisattva.
This person daily attains the perfect merit of the six pāramitās and acquires an inexhaustible eloquence and a mass of pure wisdom.
The breath emitted from their mouth touches the bodies of others.
Those who are touched by it shall be freed from the poison of all anger and shall attain the rank of a Bodhisattva.
Suppose that all the people of the four continents were to attain the rank of a Bodhisattva of the seventh stage.
The merits possessed by all those bodhisattvas are equal and no different from the merit of reciting this six-syllable mantra once.
This mantra is the subtle and wondrous fundamental mind of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
If a person transcribes these six syllables of the Great Mantra,
it is equivalent to transcribing the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma;
the merit obtained is equal and no different.
If one were to fashion images of the Tathāgata out of gold and jewels as numerous as motes of dust,
it would not equal the merit of writing down even a single character from among these six syllables.
If a person attains this six-syllable mahāvidyā, [they shall obtain all benefits].
Such a person cannot be defiled by greed, anger, or delusion.
If one wears this mantra upon their body,
they likewise will not be defiled by the afflictions of greed, anger, and delusion.

All sentient beings who touch this with their hands or see it with their eyes shall swiftly attain the rank of a bodhisattva and never again undergo the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, death, and so forth.
Having finished reciting these six great syllables,
seventy-seven koṭis of Buddhas simultaneously appeared before him and,
with one voice, recited the Cundī-dhāraṇī.

One should then know that these six syllables of the Great Illumination (Ṣaḍakṣarī Mahāvidyā) are to be employed in conjunction with the Cundī Dhāraṇī in their proper sequence, as explained at length in the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-ratnarāja-sūtra*.
Thereafter, one should form the Cundī mudrā at the heart.
Having recited the Cundī mantra and the One-Syllable Mahācakra mantra together in one place one hundred and eight times, one should release the hand seal over the crown of the head;
alternatively, for those who do not prefer the Mahācakra mantra, [the same may be done].
It is also sufficient to recite only the Cundī mantra.
As for the mudrā of Cundī:
interlace the ring fingers and little fingers of both hands within.
The two middle fingers are held straight and upright, touching at their tips;
the two index fingers are bent and pressed against the first joints of the two middle fingers;
and the two thumbs pinch the middle joints of the ring fingers of the right hand.
If there is an invitation or summons, one should move the two index fingers back and forth while correctly forming the mudrā and reciting the mantra.
When wishing to keep count, one should mark it upon one's own fingers.
One may mark it on the arms of the Bhṛkuṭī Bodhisattva,
or mark it upon the heart of Avalokiteśvara;
either way, marking it ten times is effective.
Alternatively, it is even better to form the mudrā and recite one thousand and eighty times,
or one hundred and eight times;
externally, simply form the Vajra Fist Mudrā with the left hand.
It is also permissible to hold the rosary while forming the mudrā with the right hand;
however, for those who are busy, one may simply recite it without holding the beads.
The mantra of the Great Cundī Dhāraṇī, the Heart of the Mother of Seven Koṭis of Buddhas, is as follows:

*Namo bhagavate sarvatathāgatapūjita-tanaye tadyathā oṃ jvale jvale jvālani jvālani svāhā.* The Buddha said: "This mantra is able to extinguish all karmic obstacles and the ten evil deeds and five heinous crimes."
One who upholds this mantra accomplishes all the merits of pure dharmas;
it makes no distinction between those living as householders or those who have left the home life, nor does it matter whether they drink alcohol, eat meat, or have wives and children.
Without discriminating between the pure and the impure,
merely reciting this with a sincere heart can cause sentient beings with short lifespans to increase their life by immeasurable amounts.
Even the disease of kāmalā can be cured;
how much more so other ailments?
It is impossible that they would not be extinguished.
If one recites [the mantra] for a full forty-nine days,
the Bodhisattva Cundā will cause these two holy ones to constantly follow that person,
observing all their thoughts, whether virtuous or evil.
All [the deities] shall report each matter individually at one’s ear.
If there are those who lack merit or auspicious signs, who fail to attain office despite seeking it, and who are oppressed by poverty and suffering, they should constantly recite this mantra;

this will enable them to obtain the blessings of a Cakravartin in the present life, and the official positions they seek will surely be attained as desired. In the *Chanzong Chuanteng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Chan School), a former master is quoted as saying:
If one recites the three-line mantra ten million times,
one will be known as "One Who Transcends All Men.
If one seeks wisdom, one shall obtain great wisdom.
Those who seek sons or daughters shall obtain them; whatever they may seek,
there is nothing that is not fulfilled according to their wishes,
like a wish-fulfilling jewel that accords with every thought.
Furthermore, reciting this mantra can cause kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly to give rise to hearts of love and respect;
upon seeing them, they will immediately rejoice.
One who recites this mantra cannot be drowned by water.
Fire cannot burn it;
poisons, enemies, military arrays, powerful bandits,
as well as evil dragons, beasts, and various malevolent spirits, are all unable to harm it.
If one wishes to invite Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, Yama-rāja, or others, merely reciting this mantra will ensure their arrival upon invitation;
they shall not dare to disregard the sequence.
Whatever tasks one commands them to perform, they shall all be accomplished according to one's will.
This mantra possesses great power within Jambudvīpa;
it can move Mount Sumeru and dry up the waters of the great ocean.
It can cause flowers and fruit to grow upon withered, parched wood.
How much more so for one who can further recite according to the Dharma;
without changing their physical body, they shall attain great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and go to Tuṣita Heaven.
If they seek long life or various elixirs of the immortals, [they shall likewise succeed].
If one merely recites the mantra according to the ritual,
one will immediately behold Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva or Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva,
who will bestow upon one the wondrous medicine of the immortals.
Upon consuming it as one pleases, one immediately attains the Way of the Immortals.
One’s lifespan is extended to equal that of the sun and moon,
and one realizes the stage of a Bodhisattva.
If one recites [this] according to the ritual method for one million times,
one will immediately be able to travel to the pure lands of the ten directions,
serve all Buddhas in succession, universally hear the wondrous Dharma, and attain realization of Bodhi.
If one wishes to accomplish the mandala ritual,
it does not require the extensive offerings of the various sections;
rather, it is established upon ground dug and smeared with fragrant mud.
Using only a new mirror that has never been used,
on the fifteenth night of the month,
place the mirror before you facing east in front of a Buddha image while seated.
Adorn the various offering implements according to one's capacity,
burn安息香 (anxiang) incense, and prepare pure water;
thereafter, form the mudrā at the heart.
Chant the mantra over the mirror one hundred and eight times.
Place the mirror in a pouch and always carry it with you.
Whenever you wish to perform recitation, simply set the mirror-altar before you.
Form the mudrās and recite the mantra.
If one is unable to perform the recitation before a mirror every day,
one should simply do so before a mirror on the ten days of the *zhāi* (fasting) observances.

Apart from the ten days of the *zhāirì* (fasting days), one may also perform recitations before this mirror altar; among all the secret treasuries, this mirror altar is the most essential and wondrous, as it universally encompasses all altars.
If there is no mirror, one should simply visualize a single mirror before oneself and perform the recitation;
this is extensively taught in such texts as the *Pariśuddhi-sarvadurgati-śodhana-sūtra*.
Visualizing the formation of the maṇḍala while performing the recitation is considered supreme.
Alternatively, for those who are unable to visualize the maṇḍala,
they should simply focus their attention on reciting the mantra.
As for the ten days of observance (daśa-śīla):

That is to say: the first day, the eighth day, the fourteenth day, the fifteenth day, the eighteenth day, the twenty-third day, the twenty-fourth day, the twenty-eighth day, the twenty-ninth day, and the thirtieth day.
This Cundī Dhāraṇī was spoken by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas alike;
it uniquely and individually practices the mantra altar rites that comprehensively encompass the twenty-five sections.
According to the Sanskrit original, there are one hundred thousand verses explaining the text.
Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna praised it with these verses:
"Accumulation of the merits of Cundī, Those with tranquil minds should constantly recite it."
No great calamities whatsoever can invade such a person,
whether in the heavens or among humans; they shall receive blessings equal to those of a Buddha,
for having encountered this wish-fulfilling jewel, they will certainly attain the Peerless.
The details are as extensively explained in the various Cundī-sūtras and the ritual manuals of Nāgārjuna from the Vidyottama-mahātantra. Furthermore,
this Cundī is also named Cundi or Jonā, among other names.
However, it is merely that their Brahma-voices differ.
The one-syllable mantra of the Great Wheel (Mahācakra) is precisely this Vajravārāhī (Kula-vṛnda).
It is also called the One-Syllable Heart Mantra of the Final Dharma Age.
At the time of the final dharma age, when the teachings are about to perish,
this mantra possesses great power and can bring about vast benefit for the world.
It can protect the Tathāgata’s entire treasury of Dharma;
it can subdue all the eight classes of supernatural beings;
and it can destroy all evil incantations of the world.
This is the crown of all Buddhas;
it is the heart of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva;
it is able to bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
It can bestow happiness upon all sentient beings;
whoever practices it shall obtain its fruits according to their wishes,
just as a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) can satisfy every aspiration.
If one recites this mantra,
all malevolent ghosts and spirits within a radius of five hundred *yojanas* in the four directions will scatter in flight on their own accord.
None of the malevolent planetary deities or celestial māras shall dare to approach or invade [the practitioner].
If one recites any other mantra and fears it will not achieve success, one should then employ this spell together with that other mantra.
If one recites and maintains this together in a single location, accomplishment is certain.
Should it not be accomplished or if no manifest signs appear,
the mantra deities and others shall have their heads split into seven pieces.
It should be known that this mantra can assist all other mantras in swiftly attaining accomplishment.

Alternatively, by holding this mantra alone, one may also achieve extensive results, as described in the *Mañjuśrī-vidhi-sūtra* and the *Ekākṣara-hṛdaya-mantra-sūtra*. Reciting according to the sequence explained above leads up to the Cundī mantra.
If one is unable to form the Cundī mudrā,
simply make the vajra-fist mudrā with the left hand and hold the rosary with the right hand while reciting it.
Alternatively, for those who are unable to recite the sequence of mantras from the Pure Dharma Realm and so forth,
they should simply hold the Cundī-dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, for those of dull faculties who cannot fully receive this Cundī, [there is another method].
One should maintain [the mantra] starting from the syllable *oṃ* and below.
That which precedes the syllable *oṃ* is the verse of homage;
the syllable *oṃ* and those that follow are the actual mantra.
Each time the recitation is completed,
form the Vajra Fist Mudrā with the right hand and seal the five locations while reciting the HŪṂ mantra.
First seal the forehead, then the left shoulder, then the right shoulder, then the heart, and finally the throat.
Once the sealing is complete, disperse it over the crown of the head.
This can eliminate all demonic obstacles and accomplish all supreme matters.
Alternatively, it is also permissible to first seal the five places with the mudrā before beginning the recitation.
Furthermore, if one wishes to expel spirits and deities from wherever one resides,
one need only bind the Vajra-bond and recite the Cundī Dhāraṇī.
Recite the mantra over scented water twenty-one times and sprinkle it in the eight directions, above, and below;
this immediately establishes a boundary for warding off evil influences.
Furthermore, regarding the correct manner of recitation,
it accords with what is taught in several scriptural sources, such as the *Koṭi-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, the *Vajraśekhara-sūtra*, and the *Pañcākṣara-dhāraṇī-stotra*.
According to the inclinations of the faculties, there are also many types.
First is the yoga of retention (*dhāraṇī-yoga*),
which involves merely visualizing syllables arranged within the moon-disc of the mind.
One should visualize one's own mind as a single moon disc,
serene, pure, and clearly distinct within and without.
Within this moon disc, settle the mind upon the Sanskrit syllable *Oṃ*, and [surround it] with the syllables *Jñā*, *Li*, *Kṣu*, *Li*, *Jña*, *Ti*, *Svā*, and *Hā*.
From the beginning, rotate clockwise in sequence along the rim of the wheel—pronouncing the syllables with a falling tone—and when it ends, begin again.
Second is the retention of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpāna-dhāraṇī*):
this means visualizing the mantra-syllables within the incoming and outgoing breaths.
As the breath goes out, the syllables go out;
as the breath comes in, the syllables come in.
Each syllable is clearly distinct, like a string of bright pearls, without interruption. Or, when the breath goes out:
Visualize the nine sacred Brahma-syllables within the moon disc of one’s own heart;
each syllable is linked in a continuous chain, all emitting light of five colors from one’s own mouth.
It flows into the mouth of Cundī Bodhisattvā and is arranged clockwise within the moon-disc of Cundī Bodhisattvā’s heart.
This occurs when the breath enters.
Visualize the syllables within the moon-disc of the heart of Bodhisattva Cundī;
each syllable is linked like a chain and emits five-colored light that issues forth from the mouth of Bodhisattva Cundī.
It flows into one's own mouth and is arranged clockwise within the moon disc at the heart;
thus it ends and begins again.
Visualize this as being most wondrous, held by the three vajras:
without moving the lips or teeth, and without the tongue reaching the palate,
there is only subtle movement within the mouth.
Fourth is the subtle sound recitation (*sūkṣma-śabda-dhāraṇī*):
one should merely let it be heard by one's own ears;
neither too slow nor too fast, each syllable must be pronounced with clarity.
Fifth, reciting loudly so that others may hear it and thereby extinguish their transgressions.
Furthermore, there are two other ways of recitation.
First is the incalculable recitation (*asaṃkhyeyajapa*),
which means reciting constantly and without interruption without using a rosary to fix the number.
Second is recitation with counting.
This means that one must count using a rosary and establish a fixed limit for each day;
the number of recitations must not be deficient. Regarding the merit obtained from counting with a rosary, it is extensively praised in various sutras.
As stated in the *Akṣamālā-guṇa-sūtra*:
"If there is a person who holds a rosary in their hand,
even though they do not recite the names of the Buddhas or dhāraṇīs,"
This person shall also obtain immeasurable merit.
Furthermore, a verse from the *Vajraśekhara-mālā-sūtra* says:
"If one places [the mantra] upon the topknot, it purifies even the Avīci Hell."
Worn upon the crown of the head, it extinguishes the four grave offenses;
held in the hand or on the arm,
it eliminates all sins and enables the practitioner to swiftly attain purification.
Furthermore, the *Ekākṣaroṣṇīṣacakravarti-tantra* states:
"If one consecrates a rosary seven times with the mantra of the syllable *raṃ*,
it should be used when performing recitation."
Recite either once or a thousand times.
When counting with the rosary beads, if you reach the central bead (mātṛkā), you must turn back and may not pass beyond it. Every day, recite according to the ritual rules.
One must specify the time period:
if one observes it for one period, it refers to the morning;
if for two periods, it includes both the morning and evening.
If one practices during the three periods of the day, adding noon; if one is busy with affairs, there is no restriction on the time.
One should practice whenever there is leisure.
If one is of superior capacity, it is required that one be in accordance with the three secrets.
First, the secret of body: forming the mudrās.
Second, the secret of speech: reciting mantras.
Third, the secret of mind: visualizing the Sanskrit syllables of the mantra.
One may take as an object of focus the sound of recitation, or visualize the Bodhisattva Cundī,
or visualize the objects held in the Bodhisattva’s hands, such as the vajra, the flask, the flower, the fruit, and so forth; thus,
the *Commentary on the Shenbian jing* states:
If one takes the three mysteries as the gateway,
there is no need to undergo kalpas of time to fully cultivate all practices;
rather, one shall fulfill all the pāramitās within this very life.
Furthermore, while correctly reciting the mantra, one must not converse with others until one hundred and eight recitations have been completed.
If one wishes to speak, [one should do so only after the count is finished].
Visualize the single Sanskrit syllable *ṢRAṂ* (𑖮) upon your own tongue.
Even while speaking, it shall not be interrupted.
A question is asked: "Is the accomplishment of merit achieved by maintaining only a single path of mantra?"
Furthermore, regarding the accomplishment of merit through extensively upholding many versions of mantras,
there are two approaches.
The first is the approach according to the inclinations of individual faculties.
This means that there are many types of faculties (*indriya*) with differing inclinations.
Some may delight in upholding three paths, five paths, ten paths, or even a hundred paths and so forth;
in between, according to the differing inclinations of their faculties, all may obtain the power to uphold and recite [the mantras].
Second is the gateway of swiftly attaining accomplishment.
This means that if one seeks to swiftly achieve all meritorious qualities,
one should single-mindedly recite the mantra of a single path.
At the time of accomplishment, all the merits of the mantras are fully realized.
Thus, the Mañjuśrī-vidhi-sūtra states:
"If one desires the accomplishment of all merits..."
One must not give rise to thoughts that these are separate mantras.
Although there are several paths of mantras mentioned above,
they are all successive stages for the recitation of the Cundī mantra.
Question: Since one can achieve accomplishment quickly by reciting a single mantra exclusively, why is it shown that there are many Tārā mantras for people to hold and recite?
Answer: First, because Tārā universally contains all other mantras within herself.
The Cundī [Dhāraṇī] can contain all other mantras,
whereas all other mantras cannot contain the Cundī;
it is like the great ocean, which can encompass the hundred rivers.
Just as the hundred rivers are not contained within the great ocean, yet the Cundī Mantra universally encompasses all mantras, as will be explained below;
secondly, because the ritual for the Cundī altar is easy to accomplish, one should simply use a new mirror that has never been used before.
This constitutes the ritual for the altar.
It differs from the altar rituals established for other mantras;
one must select a pure location.
One should smear the ground with fragrant mud and extensively fashion images of the Buddha;
only by using many ritual implements can one achieve success.
Those who possess wealth should extensively fashion images of the Buddha and prepare many offerings.
One should arrange a mirror-mandala before an image of the Buddha and perform the recitation facing it;

this is even more excellent. As for the *Cundī* [dhāraṇī], since it may be recited regardless of whether one is defiled or pure, it may be recited by anyone—whether lay or ordained, those who drink alcohol or eat meat, or those with wives and children.
Unlike other mantras which require the observance of precepts before they can be recited and practiced,
this is intended for those among the laity whose constant occupations involve taking wives, raising children, drinking wine, and eating meat.
Although they may encounter monks who provide instruction,
their habitual tendencies are difficult to reform;
if one does not employ this great, inconceivable dharani method to rescue and liberate them, [they will remain lost].
On what day will such people as these be able to transcend birth and death?
Those who maintain the purity of fasting and precepts and recite according to the Dharma shall achieve even more sublime and wondrous results.
Therefore, the Cundī Sūtra states:
"How much more so for one who can further observe the fast and maintain the precepts,
reciting according to the Dharma without letting the body remain empty."
This refers to attaining entry into the divine powers (ṛddhipāda) upon reaching the fourth heaven; for this reason, the Cundī mantra is frequently revealed so that people may recite it.
If there are those who wish to maintain other mantras, [they may do so].
One will obtain results according to one's mind;
do not insist on adhering to a single path alone. Although you may specialize in reciting two mantras, you must first give rise to perfect faith and believe in the mantras of the five families.
All of these are gateways to attaining Buddhahood.
If one violates even a single precept, it will result in the slander of the Dharma for many others.
Furthermore, when a practitioner of True Word (Shingon) first intends to recite the mantras each day before a mirror:
Alternatively, one may simply first visualize upon the crown of one's head the Sanskrit syllable *HŪṂ* (written as 𑖮𑖽),
resembling a bright pearl;
thereafter, one performs the recitation.
Furthermore, this is taught in several dozen scriptures and treatises,
such as the *Mahāyāna-maṇḍala-bhāvanā-sūtra*,
the *Vidyādharapiṭaka-siddhi-vidhi-sūtra*, and the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-yoga-dharma-sādhana*.
Alternatively, one may visualize the syllable *Ṛ* atop one's own head,
which transforms into a triangular wheel of fire that burns the body from the crown of the head down to the feet until it is completely consumed.

Pervading the entire Dharma-realm, one sees only purity; even if one has committed the five sins of immediate retribution, by burning the body with these syllables, they are all extinguished without remainder. Next, visualize the single Brahmi letter *A* (𑀅) arising as one’s own body, meaning that the letter *A* is itself the essence of the signless Dharma-realm.
From the signless dharma-realm, one generates the body of the practitioner;
then, one visualizes the syllable *Aṃ* at the crown of one's head, within the junction of the ten directions.
One should understand that this syllable *Aṃ* is itself the essence of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
The water of the Dharma of radiant light is used to sprinkle upon the crown of the Buddha-son’s head;
this is the secret initiation method (*guhyābhiṣeka-dharmamukha*), after which one should perform the recitation.
Alternatively, one may visualize one's own heart as a single moon disc, perfectly full and pure.
Within the lunar disc is the syllable *Oṃ* in Brahmī script. Although the Tathāgata practiced the path for many years during his stage as a bodhisattva, he did not attain enlightenment;
however, by later practicing this visualization, he attained perfect awakening during the first watch of the night.
This refers to the syllable Oṃ, which encompasses immeasurable dharma-gates and is the mother of all mantras;

all Tathāgatas attain Buddhahood by means of meditating upon this syllable. Alternatively, one may visualize the syllable A within the lunar disc of the mind, for the syllable A is the body of Vairocana Buddha.
This is both the *dharmadhātu* and the bodhicitta.

If a person contemplates it, they can generate immeasurable merit; or, one may visualize the syllable *HŪṂ* within the lunar disc of the mind—this syllable *HŪṂ* is said to encompass all mantras of the Vajra family.
This is the body of the Lord of the Vajra Family;
if one constantly contemplates it,
it can eliminate all karmic obstacles and hindrances.
To accomplish all meritorious qualities, one should either visualize the syllable *ḹṃ* on the tongue,
or visualize the syllable *hūṃ* and then recite the mantra;
or one should visualize a great lotus flower emerging from the neck of one's own body.
Upon the lotus, the syllable *A* appears.
One should further visualize that the syllable *A* transforms into a moon disc (*candramaṇḍala*).
Then, one should further visualize that the moon disc transforms into the syllable *HŪṂ*.
The syllable HŪṂ transforms into a five-pronged vajra.
Visualize this vajra moving onto the tongue;
only then is it called the "vajra tongue."
Then, while reciting, one should also visualize the syllable *A* within both hands.
The syllable *A* transforms into a moon disc (*candramaṇḍala*),
and the moon disc transforms into the syllable *HŪṂ*.
The syllable HŪṂ transforms into a white five-pronged vajra;
only then is one named Vajrapāṇi.
Thereafter, one should form all mudrās or visualize the nine sacred Brahma-syllables of Cundā.
Each individual syllable possesses various kinds of light,
which are to be placed within one's own body parts.
Specifically, one should visualize the syllable Oṃ placed upon the head.
Place the syllable *Ccha* on the two eyes;
place the syllable *Lle* on the neck;
place the syllable *Jhu* at the heart.
Place the syllable *ṢṬRĪ* on both shoulders;
place the syllable *ZVAṄ* in the center of the navel;
and place *TI* at the feet.
Once the visualization has been established, one should then perform the recitation as explained in the *Vidyādharapiṭaka-vidhi-sūtra*.
For those who seek accomplishment within the practice of the Bodhisattva Cundī,
they should first contemplate the fundamental, subtle wheel of syllables of the Bodhisattva Cundī.
One’s own body and its various parts will become clearly manifest;
all sinful karma created in previous lives will be entirely extinguished,
and whatever one seeks will certainly be accomplished.
The arrangement of these nine syllables is explained in several places within the *Tripiṭaka*.

The merits of visualizing these Sanskrit syllables are described in detail as they appear in various *dhāraṇī* sūtras. This concludes the above section on the visualization gate of the Sanskrit syllables.
If one constantly contemplates this during the four modes of conduct, it is even more sublime. Generally speaking, whenever various sutras mention the visualization of mantra syllables,
these are all in Sanskrit characters,
not the characters of this land.
Therefore, the *Ekākṣara-uṣṇīṣa-cakra-rāja-tantra-vidhi* states: "Regarding what is called 'contemplating all syllables,' one should gaze solely upon the Brāhmī script;
it does not refer to the scripts of various regions."
There is the power of great divine efficacy.
Some may be unable to visualize the Brahma-syllables;
yet, by merely reciting with single-minded devotion, one will likewise possess all samādhis.
Therefore, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states:
"Dhāraṇī is the treasury of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*),
for hundreds of thousands of samādhis constantly manifest before one."
If, when one is reciting with intense urgency,
one encounters various demonic obstacles, or suddenly feels fear,
or finds it difficult to maintain the recitation with the tongue, or experiences unease in body and mind.
Or if one has much anger or much sleep, or perceives various unusual signs,
or develops a contrary doubt toward the mantra and does not wish to recite it, and so forth—
if these are to be remedied:
One should contemplate the letter *ra* (𑀭) of the Brahmī script, whereby that realm will naturally be extinguished.
If discursive thought is excessive,
one should contemplate the letter *sa* (𑀲).
This immediately becomes non-conceptualization.
If there is an abundance of attachment to the mind of existence,
one should contemplate the syllable *haṃ*.
This is because the dharma of dependent origination is fundamentally empty. The above explanation has been given according to one particular approach;
however, to speak of it in its true nature, any single character may be employed in all instances.
This means that a single syllable truly possesses all syllables and all functional capacities;
it is the very essence of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Question: Why do the Sanskrit syllables all possess such inconceivable and divine efficacy?
Answer: It is said that each and every syllable is itself the essence, for it is the very body and mind of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
furthermore, this essence is the dharma-dhātu, which is free from all characteristics.
Furthermore, because its very essence consists of the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit, it possesses inconceivable divine efficacy;
these Sanskrit characters of the Western Heaven exist inherently by the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
They were merely transmitted by the Brahmā King at the time of the world’s initial formation.

The characters of this land [China] were not created by Cang Jie and others; if that were so, then all the Sanskrit characters of the Western Heaven should likewise possess inconceivable divine efficacy.
Why, then, do you single out only the characters within mantras?
The answer is: it refers to the syllables within the mantra.
This is because all Buddhas, by their inconceivable power, sustain them through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), and because the nature of phenomena is thus.
There is a particular spiritual efficacy in such vernacular expressions as "This is the One" and "Urgently according to the Law and Command" (jìjí rú lùlìng).
A mantra-spoken fire does not burn, and mantra-spoken water does not heat.
This is because the power of incantatory speech possesses a specific efficacy;
it is not the case that all other forms of speech possess such efficacy.
The same applies to letters in the Western [Sanskrit] tradition.
Although the letter is one and the same, it is said that certain syllables within mantras possess a specific divine efficacy,
whereas not all other letters possess such divine efficacy.
Question: As stated above, the practices of facing the altar, binding mudrās, and reciting mantras—would these not be "with signs" (sanimitta)?
Answer: Within the essence of the non-obstructive Dharmadhātu of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), [there is no such distinction].
The inexhaustible dharma-gates are inherently complete;
the formless dharma-gate of the Chan school is merely one gate within these inexhaustible gates.
Now, the mudrās and mantras of the Esoteric Vehicle’s altar rituals are, in their very essence, the unobstructed Dharma-realm;
this is as explained in the "Entrance of Manifesting the Dharma by Relying on Phenomena" within the Ten Mysterious Gates of the *Huayan jing shuchao*.
The Golden World is the fundamental nature;
Maitreya’s pavilion is the Dharma-gate;
and the fire-pit and mountain of blades of the Brahmin Jvalanānta.
This refers precisely to the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of prajñā and so forth.
Now, there are those who say that reciting mantras,
forming mudrās, and facing the altar are merely attachments to signs (*nimitta*).
This refers specifically to the Chan school;
it means seeking the signless externally while remaining apart from signs.
The ancient masters pointed this out as a view of the non-Buddhists;
it is not the intent of Buddhism.
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra-śāstra* states:
Holding and reciting divine mantras can ward off all evils and gather all manner of goodness;
yet the ignorant and the deluded do not understand this principle.
When they see one who holds the mantras, [they treat them with contempt].
Frequently, people raise slander, claiming that this is not true cultivation;
yet there has never been a single Buddha who attained the Way and delivered sentient beings without relying on divine mantras.
Please examine this closely in order to reform these defects.
A question is asked: The various masters of antiquity cited above all state that mantras are the secret dharma of all Buddhas.
This is not something understood at the stage of a causal practitioner.
Why, then, do you explain as before that the letter *A* is the body of Vairocana Buddha,
and that the letter *Hūṃ* represents the three gates of liberation and so forth?

The answer states: According to Xianshou’s *Commentary on the Heart Sūtra* and his *Commentary on the Manifestation of Power*, there are two gates for discerning the meaning of the various dhāraṇī sūtras of the Secret Treasury.
The first is the Gate of the Ineffable.
This means that mantras are the secret dharmas of all Buddhas,
transmitted from Buddha to Buddha and not open to interpretation by others;
one should simply recite and uphold them without the need for forced exegesis.
Second is the gate of forceful exposition.
This refers to taking up any single syllable from within a mantra and explaining it with sovereign mastery—
whether as a person or as a ritual action— encompassing all things horizontally and vertically.
To state the essential point:
when the inexhaustible dharma-gates are fully explained within a single syllable,
only then does one possess the true meaning of a *dhāraṇī* syllable.
In this regard, even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were to speak together for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
they could not exhaustively explain the meaning contained within a single syllable of a mantra.
How much more so for others?
Even for the speaker it is difficult, let alone for the recipient;
therefore, I shall explain but a small portion within a single syllable.
Alternatively, one may explain them by taking them as persons or as dharmas.
It was previously stated that the letter A is the body of Vairocana Buddha,
and the letter HŪṂ represents the three gates of liberation and so forth.
This is merely a forced explanation of one particular aspect of a small portion [of the meaning].
Other passages contain texts that explain the meaning of the syllables and phrases of mantras;
these are all but a small portion of one path within this very system of forced explanation. Regarding even a single syllable of a mantra:
To provide explanations consisting of two meanings, five meanings, ten meanings,
or even up to a hundred meanings and so forth,
is called the "limited meaning."
If one were to provide an explanation based on a single meaning, it would merely be a "one-sided" interpretation.

As for the previous statement that "this is known only by the Buddha and does not extend to the understanding of others," this refers to the teaching of the "inexpressible gate" according to the fundamental school of Esoteric Buddhism. This is the meaning of that inexpressible gate.
This section on the "door of forced exposition" shall manifest the perfectly transcendent ocean of results beyond words;
it shall manifest the perfectly inclusive portion of causes accompanied by words.
Question: There may be sentient beings who wish to eliminate various calamities and obstacles;
or who wish to increase their merit and wisdom;
or who wish to pray for the realization of the fruits of sainthood, and so forth.
"Should one recite solely according to the previous ritual manual,
or is there yet another method?
He replied, "One should simply recite according to the previous ritual manual."
Whatever one seeks shall be decisively accomplished.
For those who prefer to perform specific rites for each particular object of their pursuit,
I shall now briefly indicate the ritual procedures.
This is based on the *Sādhana-vidhi-sūtra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with a Thousand Hands and Thousand Eyes*,
the *Saptakoṭi-mahāvidyā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
the *Commentary on the Sūtra of Miraculous Transformations*, and various other mantra rituals and manuals.
There are five kinds of maṇḍala rites:
namely, the rite for pacifying calamities, the rite for increasing prosperity,
the rite for winning affection, and the rite for subjugation.
Regarding supramundane dharmas:
if they are performed as rites for pacifying calamities (*śāntika*), they serve to eliminate obstacles such as evil karma, grave offenses, afflictions (*kleśa*),
and various misfortunes, including legal troubles and verbal disputes.
For those afflicted by malevolent spirits or oppressed by evil stars,
the practitioner should face north and sit with legs crossed and knees raised.
The image faces south.
Before the image of Cundā, one should arrange a mirror-maṇḍala and further visualize a white circular maṇḍala.
Within this circular maṇḍala, one should visualize everywhere the syllable *vāṃ* or the syllable *hrīḥ*.
Visualize the honored image, the ritual implements, and one's own person all together within a circular mandala;
alternatively, it is also permissible to simply smear and wipe a single circular mandala before the image.
Visualize Cundī as white in color;
the flowers, fruits, food, and drink offered,
as well as one's own clothing, should all be visualized as white.
Use white sandalwood for the unguent;
use aloeswood for the incense;
and light lamps of ghee.
In conjunction with a mind of loving-kindness,
one begins on the first day of the month during the first watch of the night,
continuing until the completion of the eighth month.
Three times each day he bathes and three times he changes his clothes.
When the full period has elapsed, he either fasts or consumes the "three white foods"—
namely, milk, curd, and non-glutinous rice.
Alternatively, for those who lack the strength to prepare gruel,
it is sufficient to visualize the sacred images, ritual implements,
and robes through the power of mental concentration.
Following this principle, one should understand that when performing recitation,
after reciting the preceding sequence up to the Cundī-dhāraṇī one hundred and eight times, [one should proceed].
Thereafter, one should recite it starting only from the syllable *Oṃ*.
The sublime words are:
*Oṃ cale cule candre amuka-pāpa-vināśani svāhā*. If reciting for oneself, [the name] is placed above the word *svāhā*.
If it is for oneself, one mentions one's own name and the matter at hand;
if it is for another,
one mentions that person's name and the matter at hand.
If one performs rites of augmentation (*puṣṭika*), it is for the sake of seeking the promotion of official rank and honor, the increase of lifespan,
as well as seeking merit, intelligence, retinues, power, abundant wealth,
and the ripening of grain and wheat.
As well as seeking hidden treasures, wish-fulfilling jewels, elixirs of immortality, the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*),
and so forth. The practitioner sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) facing east,
while the image faces west.
In front of the image of Cundī, arrange a mirror-maṇḍala and further visualize a yellow square maṇḍala.
Within that square maṇḍala, visualize everywhere the syllable *A* (𑀅) or the syllable *Am* (𑀅𑁂).
Visualize both the sacred image and its ritual implements,
as well as one's own person, together within a square mandala;
alternatively, it is also permissible to merely smear and wipe out a single area directly before the image.
Visualize Cundī as yellow;
the flowers, fruits, food, drink,
and even one’s own clothing that are offered should all be visualized as yellow.
For the unguent, use white sandalwood mixed with a small amount of saffron.
Burn white sandalwood incense and light lamps of sesame oil,
maintaining a mind imbued with joy.
Beginning from the first appearance of the sun on the ninth day of the month until the full moon on the fifteenth day,
one shall bathe and change clothes three times daily, as prescribed previously.
When the period is complete, one should follow the previous instructions regarding fasting and the three white foods;
the recitation is as before.
The *Miaoyan* (Wondrous Words) says:

Oṃ cili cili cinti, may [Name] obtain all that is sought according to their wishes, svāhā. Regarding the invocation of the name and the specific ritual procedures, they are to be understood as conforming to what has been stated previously.
If one performs the rite of attraction (*vaśīkaraṇa*), it is for the purpose of seeking the protection of all noble beings and the joy of the eight classes of gods, nāgas, and others.
Furthermore, they seek eloquence in preaching the Dharma with speech and tones that are refined and pure, so that those who hear them are filled with joy;
and they seek to be respected and loved by all people, as well as to have friends and associates who draw near to them, and to bring even enemies into harmony.
The practitioner faces west and assumes the bhadrapīṭha posture,
while the image faces east.
Before the image of Cundā, one should arrange a mirror-altar and further visualize another altar in the shape of a red crescent moon.
Within the crescent-shaped mandala, one should visualize the syllable *Ha* or *Ham* pervading it.
One should imagine that the honored image, the ritual implements,
and one's own person are all contained within the crescent-shaped mandala.
Alternatively, one may simply smear and wipe a half-moon-shaped altar before the image; this is also permissible.
Visualize Cundī as having a crimson body and wearing scarlet robes.
As for the flowers, fruits, food, and drink offered:
Furthermore, one's own clothing shall all be red in color;
use saffron for unguents,
and for incense, burn a mixture of clove, storax, and honey.
However, for all fruit-oil lamps,
one should begin from the latter part of the night on the sixteenth day, while maintaining a mind associated with joy and anger.
When the twenty-third day is reached,
